question: Which statement is true for every convex function?
options: It has exactly one minimum point
Every local minimum is also a global minimum
Its derivative is always positive
It is a polynomial
explanation: Convexity guarantees that any local minimum is global. It does not guarantee a unique minimizer (that needs strict convexity) or a positive derivative.

question: Which of these 1D functions is convex everywhere?
options: sin(x)
explanation: x^2 + 5 has second derivative 2 > 0 everywhere. sin and x^3 change curvature, and x^4 - 3x^2 has negative curvature near 0.

question: How do you certify that a twice-differentiable multivariable function is convex?
options: Check that its gradient is zero somewhere
Check that its Hessian is positive semidefinite (all eigenvalues >= 0) everywhere
Check that it has a single critical point
Check that it is bounded below
explanation: A twice-differentiable function is convex if and only if its Hessian is positive semidefinite at every point.

question: Why is the MSE loss of linear regression convex in the weights?
options: Because the targets are real numbers
Because its Hessian (2/n) X^T X satisfies v^T X^T X v = |Xv|^2 >= 0 for every v
Because gradient descent converges on it
Because it has no bias term
explanation: X^T X is always positive semidefinite since v^T X^T X v is a squared norm. So the MSE Hessian has no negative curvature in any direction.

question: Two features in your linear regression are exact copies. What happens to the MSE loss?
options: It becomes non-convex
It stays convex but is no longer strictly convex, so many weight vectors achieve the same minimum
It has no minimum
Gradient descent always diverges
explanation: X^T X becomes singular (a zero eigenvalue), so there is a flat direction: weight can move between the duplicate features without changing the loss.

question: Why does scikit-learn's KMeans have an n_init parameter while LogisticRegression does not?
options: KMeans is slower
The k-means objective is non-convex, so different starts reach different local minima; logistic loss is convex
LogisticRegression uses random initialization internally
KMeans is a supervised model
explanation: With a non-convex objective, the result depends on the starting point, so k-means runs several initializations and keeps the best. Convex logistic loss reaches the same optimum from any start.
